title: The two-list morning: must and may
description: One list for what truly must happen today, one for what may. A five-minute morning habit that ends the guilt of the endless to-do list.

body.heading: Why the long list fails
paragraphs: A single long to-do list mixes the urgent with the imaginary: beside 'call the dentist' sit 'reorganise the garage' and 'learn Italian', all wearing the same importance. By evening, three things are done and seventeen are not, and the day feels like a failure that arithmetic created.
The problem is not your effort. It is that the list never told the truth about what a day can hold.

body.heading: Must, then may
paragraphs: Each morning, write two lists. The Must list gets at most three items — the things that genuinely have to happen today, small enough to be finishable. The May list gets everything else: welcome, visible, and carrying no guilt whatsoever. Mays are opportunities, not obligations.

Work the Musts first. When they are done — and on a well-built list, they usually are by mid-afternoon — the day is officially a success, and every May you touch afterwards is a bonus you chose, not a debt you serviced.

body.heading: Keep the lists honest
paragraphs: A Must that survives three mornings un-done is telling you something: it is too big (split it), it needs someone else (ask), or it does not actually matter (let it go, in writing, on purpose).
Five minutes, two lists, three Musts. The day stops being a verdict on your character and goes back to being a day.

takeaway: Three honest Musts and a guilt-free list of Mays: finish the Musts and the day counts as a success, whatever else happens.
